content: The incidence of seizures following supratentorial craniotomy for non-traumatic conditions is estimated to range between 15% and 20%. However, the risk of experiencing a seizure can vary widely, from 3% to 92%, over a five-year period. Postoperative seizures are most likely to occur within the first month after cranial surgery and can lead to the development of epilepsy. The use of antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) as a preventive measure, either before or after surgery, has been studied in several randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of AEDs when used prophylactically in patients undergoing craniotomy and to identify which AEDs are most effective. For this updated review, databases such as the Cochrane Epilepsy Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP) were searched on September 29, 2019. No language restrictions were applied. The review included RCTs involving patients without a history of epilepsy who underwent craniotomy for therapeutic or diagnostic purposes. Trials with adequate randomization and concealment methods, whether blinded or unblinded, were included. There was no minimum treatment period required, and trials using either active drugs or placebo as controls were considered. Three authors independently selected trials, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias. Disagreements were resolved through discussion. The outcomes assessed included the number of participants experiencing seizures (early seizures occurring within the first week post-craniotomy and late seizures occurring after the first week), the number of deaths, and the number of participants experiencing disability or adverse effects. Due to the heterogeneity of the trials, a meta-analysis was not performed, and the findings were presented narratively. Visual comparisons of outcomes were displayed in forest plots. The review included 10 RCTs involving a total of 1815 participants, published between 1983 and 2015. Five trials compared AEDs with placebo or no treatment. Among these, two trials demonstrated a statistically significant reduction in early seizure occurrence with AED treatment compared to controls, while the other trials showed no clear or statistically significant differences. None of the head-to-head comparisons of AEDs (e.g., phenytoin versus sodium valproate, phenytoin versus phenobarbital, levetiracetam versus phenytoin, zonisamide versus phenobarbital) showed statistically significant differences in preventing either early or late seizures. Only five trials reported data on mortality. One trial found significantly fewer deaths in the carbamazepine and no-treatment groups compared to the phenytoin group after 24 months of treatment, but this difference was not observed at six months. Adverse effects were poorly reported across the trials. However, three trials indicated that phenytoin was associated with significantly more adverse events compared to valproate, placebo, or no treatment. None of the trials reported outcomes related to functional disability. The evidence was judged to be of low certainty for all reported outcomes due to methodological limitations and variability in the comparisons made across trials. The authors concluded that there is limited and low-certainty evidence to suggest that prophylactic AED treatment is effective or ineffective in preventing postcraniotomy seizures, whether early or late. The current evidence base is constrained by methodological inconsistencies and poor reporting of outcomes such as mortality and adverse events. High-quality, contemporary trials are needed to better assess the clinical effectiveness of prophylactic AEDs compared to placebo, no treatment, or other AEDs in preventing postcraniotomy seizures in this specific patient population.
